lead: A blurred photograph is the true image multiplied by a blur kernel H in the frequency domain, plus noise. Inverse filtering divides the observed spectrum by H and recovers the image when H is strong. It explodes where H is small, because noise is divided by the same small number. The Wiener filter adds a noise-to-signal term to the denominator, so it trusts the data only where H is large. These filters are used in microscopy, astronomy, medical imaging and restoring old photographs.
prereq: You need: 3.1 for H, 3.2 for noise power, and the DFT from Unit 2.

blocks.text: Write the frequency-domain degradation model as G(u,v) = H(u,v)F(u,v) + N(u,v). G, F and N are the DFTs of the observed image, the true image and the noise. H is the degradation transfer function. u and v are frequency indices. The inverse filter estimates the true spectrum by dividing: F̂ = G/H. Substitute the model: F̂ = F + N/H. The image spectrum passes through unchanged. The noise spectrum is multiplied by 1/H.

blocks.where: F̂ is the estimated image spectrum; G is the observed spectrum; H is the degradation transfer function; F is the true spectrum; N is the noise spectrum.

blocks.text: At |H| = 1, noise passes unchanged. At |H| = 0.01, noise is multiplied by 100. At a zero of H the division is undefined, and numerical noise produces a huge value. Inverse filtering therefore needs a high signal-to-noise ratio and an H with no zeros in the band.

items: Pad H to the image size.
Take the DFT of the observed image.
Divide point by point by H.
Keep the real part and clip to the display range.

blocks.text: The Wiener filter chooses F̂ to minimise the mean square error E[|F − F̂|²] in the frequency domain, which equals the spatial-domain error E[(f − f̂)²]. Here F and F̂ are complex spectra, so the modulus squared is taken. Its frequency-domain form adds a noise-to-signal term to the denominator, so the filter backs off where H is small.

blocks.where: F̂ is the estimated spectrum; H is the degradation transfer function; H<sup>*</sup> is its complex conjugate; |H|² = HH<sup>*</sup>; S<sub>n</sub> is the noise power spectrum; S<sub>f</sub> is the image power spectrum; G is the observed spectrum.

blocks.text: H<sup>*</sup> is the complex conjugate of H. |H|² = HH<sup>*</sup>. S<sub>n</sub> is the noise power spectrum, the average |N|². S<sub>f</sub> is the image power spectrum, the average |F|². The ratio S<sub>n</sub>/S<sub>f</sub> is the local noise-to-signal ratio.

Two limits show the behaviour. For K = S<sub>n</sub>/S<sub>f</sub> > 0, the gain is H<sup>*</sup>/(|H|² + K). At H = 0 this gain is 0, because the numerator H<sup>*</sup> is 0 and the denominator is K > 0. Frequencies with no image information are suppressed instead of amplified. In the noiseless limit K = 0, the Wiener formula becomes H<sup>*</sup>/|H|² = 1/H for H ≠ 0, the inverse filter. At H = 0 it is 0/0 and must be treated separately; the ideal inverse is undefined there.

S<sub>f</sub> is unknown in practice, so replace S<sub>n</sub>/S<sub>f</sub> by a constant K. For real H the gain is H/(H² + K). Its magnitude peaks at |H| = √K, where the value is 1/(2√K). Small K gives sharpness but noise; large K gives smoothness but blur.
Constrained least squares replaces the fixed ratio by a smoothness penalty; it is the same regularised division.

Estimate H from a calibration target, a known motion path, or a physical model. Estimate K from noise variance and image variance, then tune it by trial. Pad H to the image size before the FFT; a short H array used directly causes circular wrap-around and ringing. After the inverse FFT, take the real part and clip to the display range. Filter colour images channel by channel, or filter luminance only. Check flat regions: if noise is visible, increase K. Check edges: if they look soft, decrease K. A small K keeps edges but leaves grain; a large K removes grain but softens edges. The Wiener filter needs H, so it cannot fix an unknown blur; for that use blind deconvolution. For an N-pixel image the FFT cost is O(N log N). K is a tuning knob, not a fixed law.

figure.caption: Gain against |H| for K = 0.001. The inverse gain runs off the top of the plot (1/|H| = 100 at |H| = 0.01), while the Wiener gain starts at 0, peaks at 15.811 near |H| = 0.0316, then follows 1/|H|.

spec.aria: Line plot of filter gain against |H| from 0 to 0.2: the inverse gain rises past the top of the plot as |H| falls, reaching 100 at |H| = 0.01, while the Wiener gain starts at 0, peaks at 15.811 at |H| = 0.0316, and then drops to 4.878 at |H| = 0.2.

examples.question: A blurred image has a known real H(u) row. The noise-to-signal ratio is K = 0.001. For |H| = 1, 0.1, 0.01 and 0, compute the inverse gain 1/|H| and the Wiener gain |H|/(|H|² + K). Also find the peak Wiener gain.
steps: At |H| = 0: inverse gain is undefined (infinite). Wiener gain = 0/(0² + 0.001) = 0.
examples.answer: The gains are dimensionless: at |H| = 0.01 the inverse gain is 100.000 and the Wiener gain is 9.091; at |H| = 0 the inverse gain is infinite and the Wiener gain is 0; the Wiener peak is 15.811.
examples.check:
import math
K = 0.001
for h in [1.0, 0.1, 0.01]:
    print(round(1/h, 3))
    print(round(h/(h*h + K), 3))
print(round(0.0/(0.0 + K), 3))
h = math.sqrt(K)
print(round(h/(h*h + K), 3))

traps: Dropping H<sup>*</sup> in the Wiener numerator: the numerator is the complex conjugate, not |H| or H².
Letting K be negative. K is a power ratio S<sub>n</sub>/S<sub>f</sub>, so it must be zero or positive.
Forgetting to pad H to the image size before the FFT. A short H causes circular wrap-around and ringing.
Treating the inverse gain at H = 0 as infinite in code. Division by zero gives an error or an overflow value, not a useful image.
Mixing S<sub>n</sub> and S<sub>f</sub>: S<sub>n</sub> is noise power, S<sub>f</sub> is image power, and the ratio is noise-to-signal.

quiz.q: State the inverse filter in the frequency domain.
quiz.a: F̂(u,v) = G(u,v)/H(u,v), where G is the observed spectrum and H is the degradation transfer function.

quiz.q: Why does inverse filtering amplify noise?
quiz.a: Because F̂ = F + N/H. The noise spectrum N is multiplied by 1/H. Where |H| is small, 1/|H| is large, so noise is amplified.

quiz.q: For |H| = 0.2 and K = 0.004, compute the inverse gain and the Wiener gain.
What happens to the Wiener gain as K tends to 0 and as K tends to infinity?
quiz.a: As K tends to 0, the gain tends to 1/H for H ≠ 0, the inverse filter. As K tends to infinity, the gain tends to 0, so the output is smoothed and noise is suppressed.

quiz.q: Define H<sup>*</sup>, S<sub>n</sub> and S<sub>f</sub> in the Wiener filter.
quiz.a: H<sup>*</sup> is the complex conjugate of H. S<sub>n</sub> is the noise power spectrum. S<sub>f</sub> is the image power spectrum.

quiz.q: Find the peak Wiener gain for K = 0.01.
For K > 0, why does the Wiener gain become zero at H = 0 instead of infinite?
quiz.a: For K > 0, the numerator has H<sup>*</sup>, which is zero when H is zero, while the denominator |H|² + K = K > 0. So the gain is zero. The filter does not amplify noise at frequencies with no image information.

quiz.q: Why is the constant-K form used in practice?
quiz.a: The true image power spectrum S<sub>f</sub> is unknown. Replacing S<sub>n</sub>/S<sub>f</sub> by a constant K gives a usable filter with one tuning knob.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern deconvolution uses Richardson–Lucy iteration, blind deconvolution that estimates H and F together, and learned priors from CNNs. In smartphone photography, regularised division runs on raw frames before demosaicing. Search for Wiener deconvolution, blind deconvolution, and Richardson–Lucy deconvolution.
